A pronoun like it or this needs a clear antecedent, the noun it points back to. Attribution means naming whose idea or detail it is, such as Baldwin's version or Riordan's retelling. Phrases like this portrayal, this shift, and this interpretation work well only when the sentence before them has named that portrayal, shift, or interpretation. An intensive pronoun, like himself or herself, adds emphasis. It never replaces the subject. We say Percy himself chooses, not Percy chooses himself, unless he truly chooses himself."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read each sentence. Decide whether the pronoun's antecedent is clear. Then revise with a partner."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Sentence 1: In the novel and the myth, she is shown as dangerous. This makes readers think about it differently.\nSentence 2: Perseus uses the shield and Percy uses a reflecting surface. They both work.\nSentence 3: Percy chooses to look away and fight by watching the reflection, and he did the planning myself."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In Sentence 1, who is she, and what does this point back to? How could we fix it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"She could be Medusa or Aunty Em, and this doesn't point to one clear idea. Fix: In Riordan's retelling, Medusa is shown as dangerous but also tragic. This portrayal makes readers feel some sympathy for her."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In Sentence 2, what is unclear about They both? What should we name?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They could mean the heroes or the tools. Fix: In Baldwin's myth, Perseus uses a polished shield, and in Riordan's novel, Percy uses a reflecting surface. Each tool lets the hero see Medusa safely."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Sentence 3 misuses an intensive pronoun. How should it read?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Myself doesn't match the subject he. It should be: Percy himself plans the attack, or Percy plans the attack. Intensive pronouns have to match the noun they emphasize."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Post these frames for the writing block: In [author]'s version, ___. This portrayal ___. In contrast, ___ himself/herself ___. Remind students that this must be followed by a noun (this portrayal, this shift) so the reference is never vague."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners see how pronouns and attribution phrases keep a comparison clear, and begin to evaluate which phrasing is clearer (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: A pronoun is a stand-in word. Then decide what each text seems to value."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Riordan's Chapter 11 treat blame for what Medusa became, and how is that different from the myth excerpt?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 11, Medusa tells a story about being punished by a god, so the gods are partly to blame for making her a monster. In the myth excerpt, Medusa is simply the monster, and the gods help the hero instead. The novel questions the gods' fairness, and the myth values heroic victory with divine help."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What stays the same in both texts?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In both, the hero uses reflection to avoid Medusa's gaze, and the gods matter because they are powerful. Use attribution (In Baldwin's version, In Riordan's retelling) and clear pronouns."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write one paragraph (5–8 sentences) that answers: How does Riordan's retelling of the Medusa episode both honor and change the traditional Perseus myth? Include at least one cited detail from Chapter 11 (pp. 178–187) and one cited detail from the Baldwin excerpt. Use at least one phrase such as this portrayal, this shift, or this interpretation with a clear antecedent. Underline it."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Sample paragraph: Riordan's retelling of the Medusa episode honors the traditional Perseus myth in some ways but changes it to ask new questions. In Baldwin's version, the gods give Perseus special gifts, and he approaches Medusa by watching her reflection so that he will not be turned to stone. Riordan keeps this idea when Percy carefully uses a reflecting surface to fight Medusa without looking at her directly (Ch. 11). However, the novel changes how readers see Medusa. In the myth excerpt, she is only a monster to defeat, but in Chapter 11 Medusa explains that a god punished her, and Percy himself thinks about her afterward. This shift makes the gods seem less fair and makes the hero's victory more complicated. Overall, Riordan honors the original adventure while suggesting that readers should think about blame and responsibility."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and confer first with students whose topic sentences only summarize. Ask: Which two things does your paragraph compare, and how do they connect? Remind students to check every this and it for a clear antecedent."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Checklist: (1) My topic sentence names how Riordan honors and changes the myth. (2) I cite evidence from both texts. (3) I explain what the evidence shows about responsibility, blame, or the gods. (4) My pronouns have clear antecedents, and I attribute ideas to the correct text. (5) My ideas are in a logical order."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a cohesive comparison paragraph with adverbials that add detail about time, manner, place, and cause (ELD.PII.6.5, ELD.PI.6.10).","sayAsk":"Say: Say your first sentence to a partner before you write.
